headline: First Nations Lead Salmon's Journey Home to Canada's Upper Columbia
meta_description: Indigenous nations in British Columbia are restoring salmon to the Upper Columbia River through ceremonial releases and the Bringing the Salmon Home initiative.
summary_short: First Nations in British Columbia are leading efforts to restore salmon to the Upper Columbia River, healing both ecosystems and Indigenous cultures severed by dams buil…
body:
In late May along the Columbia River between British Columbia's Rocky and Purcell mountains, students who have spent five months raising sockeye salmon fry in their classrooms released the fingerling fish into the water. Mark Thomas, Shuswap Band salmon chief for the Upper Columbia, guided them through a traditional ceremony—smudging with eagle wing and juniper smoke, prayers for the fish and their families—before each child sent a tiny fry downstream through a DIY funnel to the sound of drumming and traditional song. This single morning represented far more than an educational exercise. It embodied a profound reconnection: between salmon and the Indigenous peoples who have depended on them for millennia, and between a river and its purpose.

The Columbia River, which stretches 2,000 kilometers from its B.C. headwaters to the Pacific Ocean, once supported salmon runs numbering in the millions. But the 1938 Grand Coulee Dam, built without fish passage mechanisms, blocked salmon from more than half the river's length and the spawning grounds in Canada's Upper Columbia Basin. The loss devastated First Nations, erasing food sovereignty and severing cultural ties that ran generations deep.

Now, the Secwépemc, Syilx-Okanagan, and Ktunaxa nations are leading change through the Bringing the Salmon Home initiative, launched in 2019 with support from British Columbia and Canadian governments. This year alone, the Shuswap Band reached 300 students through ceremonial releases in two communities, while the Syilx-Okanagan hosted releases across three blocked watershed areas. The work rests on reciprocity—creating pathways for salmon to find their way home, as one Ktunaxa representative explained, while setting a foundation for ecological and cultural healing that colonization fractured.
quick_facts: First Nations released 1,500 sockeye salmon fry from Penticton hatchery in Upper Columbia
Grand Coulee Dam (1938) blocked salmon from over half the river's length
Shuswap Band reached 300 students through ceremonial fry releases this year
Bringing the Salmon Home initiative launched 2019 by three Indigenous nations
Columbia River once supported salmon runs numbering in the millions
